name: Grafton
headline: Grafton, village by village,
from the common to the river.
answer: Grafton is a Worcester County town of 19,664 people (2020 Census) bordering Worcester, established in 1735. Its housing runs from the 19th-century homes around Grafton Common to worker housing in its Blackstone River mill villages. Grafton station in North Grafton is on the MBTA Framingham/Worcester Line, and Routes 122, 140 and 30 cross the town.
overview: Grafton's story begins with Hassanamisco, a Christian Indian plantation established in 1654; the town itself was established in 1735. Hassanamesitt Woods, about 200 acres on Keith Hill, is believed to hold the core of that Nipmuc village, and the Trust for Public Land bought it in 2004 for transfer to the town. Grafton Common, landscaped into an elliptical park in 1843 and 1844, is still ringed by a temple-front store, a mansard-roofed store and a Second Empire commercial block.

Away from the common, Grafton spreads into villages built on water power. North Grafton, once New England Village, sits where the Quinsigamond River falls more than 50 feet in a short distance, and Saundersville, Fisherville and Farnumsville line the Blackstone River in the southwest. Benjamin Willard began making clocks in a North Grafton workshop in 1766, a legacy now kept at the Willard House and Clock Museum. Grafton station on Pine Street puts the town on the Framingham/Worcester Line, and Tufts University's Cummings School of Veterinary Medicine has its campus here.

Grafton's zoning already makes room for denser housing near the station: its bylaw includes a North Grafton Transit Village Overlay District, a Chapter 40R smart growth district, and a Village and Neighborhood Mixed Use district, and the May 12, 2025 Annual Town Meeting warrant carried amendments to both, including a clearer definition of attached single-family homes such as townhouses. The state lists Grafton as compliant with the MBTA Communities law as of October 21, 2026. The town's 2018 Housing Production Plan counted 365 units, or 5.1% of its housing, on the state's Subsidized Housing Inventory. Values have climbed: the town reports that the average single-family assessed value rose from $625,767 in FY2025 to $663,695 in FY2026.

housing.text: Grafton's 2018 Housing Production Plan, using 2012 to 2016 ACS estimates, counted 7,179 housing units: 59.3% single-family detached, 15.3% single-family attached, 12.6% in buildings of two to four units, 6.8% in buildings of five to nine and 5.4% in buildings of ten or more, with 72.3% owner occupied. Half of the stock, 3,570 units, was built before 1980. The Massachusetts Historical Commission describes Grafton Center as possibly the best-preserved 19th-century residential and institutional village in its study area, while the Blackstone River villages retain much of their 19th-century worker housing, including duplexes, boardinghouses and double-deckers; Craftsman bungalows and Colonial Revival homes followed in the early 20th century.

villages.name: Grafton Center
villages.line: The crossroads village around Grafton Common, with 19th-century homes, stores and civic buildings.

villages.name: North Grafton
villages.line: Includes the former New England Village on the Quinsigamond River, with worker housing near Factory and Second Streets; home to Grafton station.

villages.name: South Grafton
villages.line: One of the town's three postal villages, each with its own ZIP code.

villages.name: Farnumsville
villages.line: A Blackstone River mill village in the southwest of town.

villages.name: Fisherville
villages.line: A Blackstone River mill village that keeps much of its 19th-century worker housing.

villages.name: Saundersville
villages.line: A Blackstone River mill village where a cotton mill was built in 1829.

villages.name: Centerville
villages.line: A former mill site on the Quinsigamond River west of Grafton Center.

commute.text: Grafton station sits between Worcester and Westborough on the Framingham/Worcester Line, with a 382-space parking lot. Route 140 runs through Grafton Center, Route 122 crosses toward Worcester and Providence, and Route 30 links North Grafton with Westborough.

places.name: Grafton Common
places.line: The town's central green, landscaped as an elliptical park in 1843 and 1844 and framed by 19th-century buildings.

places.name: Willard House and Clock Museum
places.line: The Willard clockmakers' home at 11 Willard Street, North Grafton, showing more than 90 Willard clocks by guided tour.

places.name: Hassanamesitt Woods
places.line: About 200 wooded acres on Keith Hill, believed to hold the core of the 17th-century Nipmuc village, with trails for hiking, skiing and birdwatching.

places.name: Grafton Land Trust properties
places.line: More than two dozen protected parcels with trails, including Brigham Hill, Fletcher Reserve and Williams Woods.

places.name: Cummings School of Veterinary Medicine
places.line: Tufts University's veterinary school campus in North Grafton.

places.name: Grafton Inn
places.line: A three-story, five-bay hip-roofed building that Samuel Wood built in 1805, one of the landmarks of Grafton Center.

history.text: The Christian Indian plantation of Hassanamisco was established.
Incorporated as the Town of Grafton.
Benjamin Willard began making clocks in his North Grafton workshop.
The Blackstone Canal was completed, with three locks in Grafton, spurring mill growth along the river.
The Providence and Worcester Railroad began service through the Blackstone River villages in the southwest of town.

faq.q: What is the median home price in Grafton, MA?
faq.a: The median single-family sale price in Grafton for calendar year 2025 was $610,000, across 153 sales, unchanged from $610,000 in 2024, according to The Warren Group's MA December 2025 Sales, Prices by Town report.

faq.q: What is the property tax rate in Grafton, MA?
faq.a: Grafton's FY2026 residential tax rate is $13.69 per $1,000 of assessed value, down $0.25 from FY2025, according to the town's State of the Town message. The town reports an average single-family assessed value of $663,695 for FY2026.

faq.q: What kinds of housing are in Grafton?
faq.a: Mostly single-family: the town's 2018 Housing Production Plan counted 59.3% of units as detached single-family homes and 15.3% as attached single-family, with 72.3% owner occupied. The Blackstone River villages keep much of their 19th-century worker housing, including duplexes and double-deckers.

Zoning districts and the May 12, 2025 warrant articles (Articles 31 and 32) from https://www.grafton-ma.gov/DocumentCenter/View/16319/Spring-2025-Warrant_Final; whether those articles passed was not confirmed, and the overview says only that the warrant carried them. Assessed values and the FY2026 rate from the FY2026 State of the Town message in the April 29, 2026 Finance Committee packet (https://grafton-ma.gov/DocumentCenter/View/20064/FC-Packet-42926?bidId=), marked preliminary draft; MMA's profile shows $13.94 with no fiscal year (it matches FY2025 per the packet).
